verses.text: Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu wrote letters, and sent to Samaria, to the rulers of Jezreel, even the elders, and to those who brought up Ahab’s sons, saying,
“Now as soon as this letter comes to you, since your master’s sons are with you, and you have chariots and horses, a fortified city also, and armor,
Select the best and fittest of your master’s sons, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house.”
But they were exceedingly afraid, and said, “Behold, the two kings didn’t stand before him! How then shall we stand?”

He who was over the household, and he who was over the city, the elders also, and those who raised the children, sent to Jehu, saying, “We are your servants, and will do all that you ask us. We will not make any man king. You do that which is good in your eyes.”

Then he wrote a letter the second time to them, saying, “If you are on my side, and if you will listen to my voice, take the heads of the men who are your master’s sons, and come to me to Jezreel by tomorrow this time.” Now the king’s sons, being seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who brought them up.
When the letter came to them, they took the king’s sons and killed them, even seventy people, and put their heads in baskets, and sent them to him to Jezreel.
A messenger came and told him, “They have brought the heads of the king’s sons.” He said, “Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning.”
In the morning, he went out, and stood, and said to all the people, “You are righteous. Behold, I conspired against my master and killed him, but who killed all these?
Know now that nothing will fall to the earth of Yahweh’s word, which Yahweh spoke concerning Ahab’s house. For Yahweh has done that which he spoke by his servant Elijah.”
So Jehu struck all that remained of Ahab’s house in Jezreel, with all his great men, his familiar friends, and his priests, until he left him no one remaining.
He arose and departed, and went to Samaria. As he was at the shearing house of the shepherds on the way,

Jehu met with the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah, and said, “Who are you?” They answered, “We are the brothers of Ahaziah. We are going down to greet the children of the king and the children of the queen.”
He said, “Take them alive!” They took them alive, and killed them at the pit of the shearing house, even forty-two men. He didn’t leave any of them.

When he had departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. He greeted him, and said to him, “Is your heart right, as my heart is with your heart?” Jehonadab answered, “It is.” “If it is, give me your hand.” He gave him his hand; and he took him up to him into the chariot.
He said, “Come with me, and see my zeal for Yahweh.” So they made him ride in his chariot.
When he came to Samaria, he struck all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, until he had destroyed him, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke to Elijah.
Jehu gathered all the people together, and said to them, “Ahab served Baal a little; but Jehu will serve him much.

Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all of his worshipers, and all of his priests. Let no one be absent; for I have a great sacrifice to Baal. Whoever is absent, he shall not live.” But Jehu did deceptively, intending to destroy the worshipers of Baal.
Jehu said, “Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal!” So they proclaimed it.

Jehu sent through all Israel; and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left that didn’t come. They came into the house of Baal; and the house of Baal was filled from one end to another.
He said to him who kept the wardrobe, “Bring out robes for all the worshipers of Baal!” So he brought robes out to them.

Jehu went with Jehonadab the son of Rechab into the house of Baal. Then he said to the worshipers of Baal, “Search, and see that none of the servants of Yahweh are here with you, but only the worshipers of Baal.”

So they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had appointed for himself eighty men outside, and said, “If any of the men whom I bring into your hands escape, he who lets him go, his life shall be for the life of him.”

As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the captains, “Go in and kill them! Let no one escape.” So they struck them with the edge of the sword. The guard and the captains threw the bodies out, and went to the inner shrine of the house of Baal.
They brought out the pillars that were in the house of Baal, and burned them.
They broke down the pillar of Baal, and broke down the house of Baal, and made it a latrine, to this day.
Thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.
However, Jehu didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin, the golden calves that were in Bethel and that were in Dan.

Yahweh said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in executing that which is right in my eyes, and have done to Ahab’s house according to all that was in my heart, your descendants shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.”
But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of Yahweh, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam, with which he made Israel to sin.
In those days Yahweh began to cut away parts of Israel; and Hazael struck them in all the borders of Israel;
from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the valley of the Arnon, even Gilead and Bashan.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehu, and all that he did, and all his might, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Jehu slept with his fathers; and they buried him in Samaria. Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place.
The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.

footnotes.content: Jehu begins with a letter—not a sword, but words. Seventy sons of Ahab stand between him and the throne, and he knows it. He doesn't announce his ambitions; he lays a trap for those who shepherd the royal house. Sometimes the most dangerous moments come wrapped in polite inquiry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His letter is cunning: choose one heir and fight for his house. He flatters them with their own strength—the chariots, the fortified city, the armor they command. But he knows fear is stronger than weapons; uncertainty paralyzes. When people don't know whom to trust, they freeze.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Select the best and fittest." A clever phrase—he's asking them to identify the worthiest, knowing they'll see the trap either way. Whether they choose or refuse, Jehu has already won their hesitation. The Lord uses human nature's own turns against those who resist His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear does what swords cannot. The rulers remember Ahab and Jezebel fell before Jehu; two kings couldn't stand against him. They do not ask what is right; they ask only what will keep them alive. When fear rules, conscience sleeps.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We are your servants, and will do all that you ask." See how quickly they surrender? They've chosen submission over the throne itself. Yet there is a truth here too: sometimes wisdom is knowing when to yield to a strength greater than your own, rather than cling to a sinking house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu's second letter is crueler: send me the heads of the seventy. He lays this charge at their feet without ambiguity. Whether they obey or rebel, he has their measure now. Many servants of dark kings discover too late that loyalty is always the first thing to be betrayed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They kill all seventy and send the heads in baskets. How quickly terror hardens into action. These are the guardians who raised the royal sons; now they murder them. Desperation, not honor, guides their hands. This is what it looks like when people abandon their posts and their God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning." A public spectacle of ruthlessness. Jehu stages the scene deliberately—this is theater meant to strike terror into every heart that sees it. Power, he understands, speaks louder when accompanied by horror.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu speaks to the assembled people with a strange innocence: "I conspired against my master and killed him, but who killed all these?" He absolves himself of the slaughter while claiming credit for the coup. Watch how power rewrites truth—he made the demand, yet asks as though he were innocent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Nothing will fall to the earth of Yahweh's word." Jehu invokes Elijah's prophecy against Ahab's house. He's right—the Lord's word stood firm. Yet notice: he uses the truth of God's judgment to justify his own brutality. We can recognize God's justice and still corrupt it with our own cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu leaves no one standing—sons, officials, priests, all of Ahab's house swept away. He completes the Lord's judgment, yet his thoroughness hints at something else: a hunger for total power, not just obedience. The work of God and the work of ambition can wear the same face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He moves toward Samaria, passing through the shearing house of the shepherds. Even in his journey, Jehu stays alert, watchful. A man who rises by the sword never truly rests; he must always be watching for the next threat.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers of Ahaziah arrive, traveling innocently to greet the royal children. They know nothing of what has happened—the news has not yet spread. They step into Jehu's path unaware, speaking words that will be their last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty-two men put to death at the pit of the shearing house. Jehu's mercy is brief—"Take them alive!"—but his judgment is final. They are related to Judah's king, part of the web he's untangling. Sometimes one sin touches many; one house's fall dragging others down with it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehonadab the son of Rechab meets him on the road. Jehonadab is known for his covenant with his household to abstain from wine and dwell in tents—a man of discipline and faith. Jehu greets him warmly and asks, "Is your heart right?" A real question, seeking alignment with a righteous man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Come with me, and see my zeal for Yahweh." Jehu invites Jehonadab into his chariot—a place of honor and trust. He wants a witness to his work, someone of faith who can affirm that what he's doing serves the Lord. Yet zeal without wisdom can become something else: self-righteousness cloaked in piety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He strikes all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, completing the judgment spoken through Elijah. The work is thorough, ordained by the Lord, and undeniably terrible. God's justice came through Jehu's hands, yet Jehu's own heart was not fully turned toward the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Ahab served Baal a little; but Jehu will serve him much." A chilling boast. He's gathering the people now, speaking about Baal worship with feigned enthusiasm. He sounds like one about to become a devoted patron, when in truth he's weaving a snare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Call to me all the prophets of Baal." The command sounds urgent, almost anxious—he wants none to be absent. Then the reason: "I have a great sacrifice to Baal." But the text adds: "Jehu did deceptively, intending to destroy the worshipers of Baal." Deception for a righteous end; yet the Lord sees both the outward act and the heart's true shape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu proclaims a solemn assembly for Baal. The people believe him; they trust his word. He has earned that trust by killing Ahab's house with such force that none dare question him. Lies wrapped in power need no other proof.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the worshipers of Baal come, filling the house of Baal from one end to another. They come willingly, certain of Jehu's approval, even his participation. The idol-house swells with them, all believing they gather to honor their god. Instead, they walk into a trap set by one they trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu orders robes brought for the worshipers of Baal, as if dressing them for a sacred ceremony. He tends to their comfort, their dignity in worship. Every detail of courtesy serves his hidden purpose. Sometimes the deadliest trap wears the face of kindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu and Jehonadab walk together into the house, then Jehu commands: "Search, and see that none of the servants of Yahweh are here with you, but only the worshipers of Baal." He's drawing the net tight—making certain there are no witnesses who follow the true God, so that all who remain are guilty of idolatry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The worshipers begin their sacrifice and burnt offerings, unaware that eighty armed men wait outside. Jehu has positioned his soldiers with a terrible command: "If any of the men whom I bring into your hands escape, his life shall be for the life of him." No mercy, no possibility of flight—only death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the burnt offering is finished, Jehu gives the word: "Go in and kill them! Let no one escape." The sword falls on them in the very act of worship. They die inside their idol-house, surrounded by the symbols of their faith. Judgment and grace are not always easy to distinguish in God's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pillars of Baal's house are brought out and burned. Fire consumes what stones held up, what hands had carved. The destruction is thorough and public, a statement that Baal's throne in Israel is broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The house of Baal itself is torn down and made into a latrine, "to this day." The narrator's note marks how completely Baal's honor is trampled. A place of worship becomes a place of human waste—the ultimate desecration, a physical memory that the false god's house is worthless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel—a tremendous work, a genuine cleansing. The Lord's judgment against idolatry came through his hands, and the false god's worship was cast down. Yet victory accomplished with cunning and blood leaves its own questions unanswered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But here is the turning point: Jehu did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam. The golden calves at Bethel and Dan remained, still worshiped. He purged Baal but clung to the idolatry that had become Israel's custom. His zeal was selective, rooted not in love for the Lord alone but in his own judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord spoke to Jehu: "Because you have done well in executing that which is right in my eyes, and have done to Ahab's house according to all that was in my heart, your descendants shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation." God affirmed his work against Ahab's house, yet the promise comes with an edge—it names what he did right, not who he was.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord with all his heart. He accomplished God's judgment but did not truly follow God's way. His heart was divided; his reign was a partial obedience to a God he served only halfway. Many do the Lord's work without becoming His servants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In those days the Lord began to cut away parts of Israel. Hazael of Aram struck them in all their borders. The kingdom that Jehu seized began to shrink. His half-faith brought half-blessing; incomplete repentance leaves a people exposed to judgment they might have avoided.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the Jordan eastward—Gilead, the lands of Gadites, Reubenites, Manassites—all laid waste by Hazael's hand. The territories named mark Israel's eastern holdings, now stripped away. Geography itself becomes a record of loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler notes Jehu's acts are written in the book of the kings of Israel. His deeds are recorded, his might is acknowledged. Yet the summary carries a quiet weight: all that power, all that ruthlessness, measured and filed away in history like any king before him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria. His reign ended as all reigns end, his body laid to rest. Jehoahaz, his son, took the throne. One generation passes; another rises. The work we do in our zeal shapes what comes after, though we cannot see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehu reigned twenty-eight years. Looking back from a longer road, I see in Jehu the danger of righteous anger without a righteous heart. We can accomplish God's judgment and still miss God Himself. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful the Lord calls us not just to accomplish tasks but to surrender ourselves—heart, not merely hands—to His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
